text: When he started again, the dog did not want to leave the fire, for it knew that it was far too cold to travel. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, at a place where the snow looked perfectly solid, the man broke through and wet himself halfway to the knees. <break time="0.8s" /> He was angry at his luck, because he now had to build a fire at once and dry his socks and moccasins. <break time="0.8s" /> He built the fire under a large spruce tree, pulling twigs from the bushes and adding bigger branches as the flame grew. <break time="0.8s" /> The old timer had said that no man should travel alone in the Klondike after fifty below, but here he was, alone and safe. <break time="0.8s" /> He smiled and thought that some of those old timers were much too careful about the cold. <break time="0.8s" /> But each time he pulled a twig, he shook the tree a little, and the heavy snow on its boughs began to move. <break time="0.8s" /> Suddenly a great mass of snow fell without warning on the man and the fire, and the fire was blotted out. <break time="0.8s" /> It was as though he had just heard his own sentence of death, and for a moment he sat and stared at the spot. <break time="0.8s" /> If he had had a trail mate, he would have been in no danger now, for his partner could have built the fire.
